We start by noting that the patient is a 13‐year‐old girl with two small (6‐mm), well‐circumscribed nodules on the forearm that have been present for several years. They are described as “cystic” on initial history, then on exam they appear rubbery, slightly tender, and pink. In addition, a second similar nodule appeared later. Now let’s review the options:

• Neuroma – These lesions (often arising after trauma) typically involve regenerating nerve fibers. They occur along a nerve and are usually painful, but they tend to be unilateral rather than suddenly presenting as two nodules in one area. Moreover, their clinical picture does not match a “cystic” or tender superficial nodule on the forearm.

• Glomus tumor – Glomus tumors are known for their extremely pinpoint, well‐circumscribed, red-blue or pink appearance. They cause very sharp, paroxysmal pain and are usually less than 5 mm in size. They are most commonly found in subungual areas of the digits. The size and location ( forearm, 6 mm nodules) do not fit the classical presentation.

• Angiolipoma – Angiolipomas are benign subcutaneous tumors composed of fat and small vessels. They are often tender and can cause discomfort and a rubbery feel. However, they usually occur over the trunk rather than the extremities and, although sometimes multiple, tend to be solitary. Moreover, while they may be painful (and occasionally have a reddish hue due to their vascularity), the classic presentation of a “cystic” lesion with two identical nodules can be seen in other benign entities.

• Spiradenoma – This is a benign tumor arising from eccrine sweat glands. It typically presents in children and young adults as a small, pink, firm (sometimes “rubbery”) and painful nodule. Although usually solitary, multiple spiradenomas may occasionally occur. In our case, a single (initial) lesion that was thought to be “cystic” then had a similar one appear nearby fits well with the behavior of a spiradenoma. Moreover, the forearm is an eccrine‐rich area, making a sweat‐gland tumor in this location quite plausible.

Thus, after comparing the features, the best match for two small, tender, pink nodules in a young girl is a firm, benign adnexal tumor of eccrine origin—that is, a spiradenoma.

The final answer is \boxed{D}.

We start by noting that the patient has several pigmented skin lesions. She has six tan‐brown macules on her trunk and arms and axillary freckling—findings that can be seen in conditions like Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). However, the “red‐blue nodule under the tip of her thumbnail” that is tender, and her complaints of paroxysmal pain and cold sensitivity of that localized area, point to an underlying abnormal process in the underlying bone of that digit.

In NF1 the most common signs are the café‐au‐lait spots (which may be present from birth and enlarge with growth) and telangiectatic (axillary and inguinal) freckling. While a neurofibroma in NF1 might appear as a subungual nodule, these typically are not described as “red–blue” nor are they characteristically tender with a strong sensitivity to temperature changes.

McCune–Albright syndrome (M‒A syndrome), on the other hand, is due to a postzygotic mutation in GNAS. Its classic triad includes café‐au‐lait spots, endocrine dysfunctions, and fibrous dysplasia of bone. Fibrous dysplasia in one or more bones can cause local pain, tenderness, and an abnormal “hot” appearance—sometimes presenting as a tender, red–blue lesion that may be exacerbated by changes in temperature (i.e. cold sensitivity). In this case the red–blue nodule under the thumbnail is highly suggestive of fibrous dysplasia in the distal phalanx of the thumb.

Thus, although the presence of café‐au‐lait macules and axillary freckling might initially make NF1 a consideration, the key features of a tender, red–blue periungual nodule and associated cold sensitivity are best explained by the bone involvement (fibrous dysplasia) seen in McCune–Albright syndrome.

Therefore, among the choices given, the most likely diagnosis is:

\boxed{C}

• The patient is a 50‐year‐old woman with a progressive, painful rash over her face, trunk, extremities, including areas like the ears and nasal tip, associated with fever, arthralgia, and retiform purpura with necrosis and bullae formation.

  • This refers to a dermatophyte infection (usually a tinea infection) modified by inappropriate steroid use. It typically presents with an annular, scaly rash—not with retiform purpura, extensive necrosis, or systemic symptoms such as fever and arthralgia.

C. Warfarin-induced skin necrosis  
  • Warfarin necrosis is a cutaneous complication of anticoagulation therapy (especially in the early phase when protein C is depleted compared to other clotting factors) and classically manifests as painful, necrotic, ecchymotic lesions. However, there is no history of warfarin use here, and warfarin-induced skin necrosis is not typically associated with leukopenia—a noted abnormality in this case.

D. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)  
  • DIC usually presents with widespread small vessel thrombosis and hemorrhage, and can display a purpuric rash. However, it is typically accompanied by signs of multiorgan failure and profound changes in coagulation labs that are not described here. The distribution of the skin lesions (face, ears, and nasal tip) in DIC is not typical, and the clinical course plus leukopenia make DIC an unlikely explanation.

B. Levamisole-induced antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) vasculitis  
  • Recently, reports have emerged of cocaine in the illicit market being adulterated with levamisole, which can have effects on the vasculature and even lead to bone marrow suppression (as evidenced by leukopenia). The contaminated cocaine has been linked to a form of necrotizing vasculitis that can present with retiform purpura, areas of necrosis, bullae, systemic inflammatory response (fever, arthralgia) and an elevated ESR. This pattern fits the detailed clinical picture provided.

Therefore, based on the history of cocaine use (with known risk of levamisole adulteration), the specific pattern of skin findings, and the lab abnormalities, the most likely diagnosis is B.

Thus, the final answer is: Answer: \boxed{B}.

We’re dealing with an asymptomatic hyperpigmented rash on the back that has been present for 4 months in a 15‐year–old. The lesions are described as scaly papules that “coalesce into confluent plaques with peripheral reticulated papillomatosis.” In dermatology these findings are characteristic of a group of idiopathic, self‐limiting papular pigmented disorders. 

A brief review of the options:

• Amyloidosis cutis dyschromica (Choice A) is very rare and usually shows localized amyloid deposition (often on the upper trunk, neck, and face) but does not typically present as confluent hyperpigmented scaly papules with a reticulated pattern.

• Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis (Choice B) is a benign condition first described in children and adolescents. Although it is more frequently seen in individuals of color, it has been reported even in younger white patients. Importantly, its clinical picture is strikingly similar to that of prurigo pigmentosa.

• Prurigo pigmentosa (Choice C) classically appears as an asymptomatic, evolving hyperpigmented papular eruption on the back. Its lesions often start as discrete papules that coalesce into plaques with an irregular, reticulated border. Over time they may show a typical evolution (papular stage, reticular stage, and atrophic stage) and then resolve spontaneously. 

• Dowling-Degos disease (Choice D) is an inherited condition that can present in early childhood or adolescence with reticulate hyperpigmented macules, but its histology (degenerative changes in the basal layer and often a more focal, linear distribution) is somewhat different, and it is not as commonly described with the classic confluent hyperpigmented scaly papules seen here.

The description provided – asymptomatic rash, hyperpigmented scaly papules that coalesce to form confluent plaques with a peripheral reticulated pattern – is most typical of prurigo pigmentosa (a disorder also grouped with idiopathic reticulate papular eruptions).

Thus, the most likely diagnosis is:

     Answer:  \boxed{C}
